questions.stem: Charlie, a 34-year-old builder, has PCR-confirmed uncomplicated influenza A with a clear chest and SpO2 97% on room air. You are safety netting before he goes home from the GP clinic. Which new symptom should you tell him means calling 000, not booking a GP review?
options: A dry cough that is still there two weeks from now
Getting better, then a new fever with coloured phlegm
Breathlessness while resting, or struggling to breathe
A fever around 38 °C that is still there on day five
questions.why: Breathlessness at rest suggests hypoxia from influenza pneumonia or another serious complication, so he needs an ambulance. Breathlessness at rest, chest pain, blue lips, confusion or drowsiness mean 000. Getting worse again after improving means same-day review.
notes: A cough and tiredness lasting 1 to 2 weeks or more after influenza is expected, so this needs reassurance or routine review, not an ambulance.
Getting better and then worse again suggests secondary bacterial pneumonia, which needs same-day GP or ED review, not necessarily a 000 call.
A fever that lasts longer than expected deserves GP review, but on its own, without respiratory distress or confusion, it is not an emergency.

questions.stem: Charlie, 34, is a previously well smoker with 3 days of fever and dry cough. Influenza A is detected on PCR. T 38.0 °C, HR 94, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, chest clear. He lives with well adult housemates. What is the most appropriate treatment in general practice?
options: Supportive care only: rest, fluids, paracetamol or ibuprofen, no antiviral or antibiotic
Oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily for 5 days, with supportive care
Amoxicillin 1 g orally three times daily for 5 days, with supportive care
Supportive care, plus oseltamivir 75 mg orally daily as prophylaxis for housemates
questions.why: This is uncomplicated influenza in a healthy adult more than 48 hours from onset, so eTG advises supportive care alone. Oseltamivir is reserved for severe illness, people at higher risk of complications, or (if considered at all in healthy adults) the first 48 hours.
notes: He is beyond 48 hours from onset, not severely unwell and not in a higher-risk group, so oseltamivir would add little apart from adverse effects.
This is a viral illness with a clear chest and normal observations. There is no evidence of bacterial pneumonia, so antibiotics would not help.
Post-exposure prophylaxis is for high-risk contacts, such as unvaccinated people with risk factors or residents of aged-care outbreaks, not healthy adult housemates.

questions.stem: Charlie, 34, asks why he can't have the flu tablet his friend got. His supervising GP explains that, in healthy adults, oseltamivir helps only if started within 48 hours of symptom onset. Which mechanism of action best explains this time window?
options: Blocks haemagglutinin binding to sialic acid, stopping the virus entering cells
Inhibits neuraminidase, stopping release of new virions from infected cells
Blocks the M2 ion channel, stopping uncoating of the virus inside the cell
Inhibits viral RNA polymerase, stopping replication of the viral genome
questions.why: Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase, the enzyme that cleaves sialic acid so that progeny virions can leave the infected cell. It limits spread to new cells, which matters only while viral replication is peaking in the first 1 to 2 days.
notes: Haemagglutinin-mediated attachment is the target of vaccine-induced neutralising antibodies, not oseltamivir.
M2 blockade is how amantadine works. It is not used, because circulating influenza A is resistant and it has no effect on influenza B.
Oseltamivir does not act on the polymerase complex. Baloxavir is the drug that targets the polymerase complex, through its cap-dependent endonuclease.

questions.stem: The practice nurse is collecting Charlie's nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory PCR. He is seated with his head tilted slightly back. To reach the posterior nasopharynx safely, in which direction should the swab be advanced through the nostril?
options: Upwards towards the bridge of the nose, following the line of the nasal bones
Upwards and laterally into the middle meatus beneath the middle concha
Upwards along the nasal septum towards the roof of the nasal cavity
Straight back along the nasal floor, parallel to the hard palate
questions.why: The nasal floor runs horizontally back to the nasopharynx. Advance the swab parallel to the hard palate, at right angles to the face, to a depth of about the distance from the nostril to the tragus of the ear.
notes: Angling upwards along the nasal bones aims at the roof of the nasal cavity, so the swab misses the nasopharynx and is more painful.
The middle meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses. It is not the nasopharynx, and probing it is uncomfortable.
The roof of the nasal cavity is the thin cribriform plate of the ethmoid. Aiming there risks injury and does not sample the nasopharynx.
